svg.title: PBB-EVPN: MAC-in-MAC encapsulation, and what the core PEs have to learn compared with plain EVPN
svg.desc: Two nested rectangle diagrams. On the left, plain EVPN puts the customer frame, its destination and source MAC and payload, directly inside the outer header the core reads, so every core PE learns every customer MAC. On the right, PBB-EVPN wraps the customer frame inside a carrier header built from B-MAC addresses and an I-SID, so the core only ever learns carrier B-MACs and customer MAC changes never cross the core. A four row table compares the MACs the core must learn, the effect of customer MAC volume, the propagation of customer MAC changes and the scale each option suits. A note says the cost is another encapsulation layer, a smaller MTU and harder troubleshooting, so it is worth it only when MAC scale really is the bottleneck.
svg.text: PBB-EVPN hides the customer MACs inside carrier MACs, so the core stops caring how many there are
Same BGP control plane; the change is what the outermost header is allowed to expose
customer MACs travel in the clear
the customer frame is the thing being read
Customer MAC churn is core table churn, and a MAC move is an update for everyone.
MAC-in-MAC: a carrier frame carries the customer frame
The BEB at the edge terminates customer MACs; a customer MAC move stops at the edge.
Every customer MAC in every EVI
Only the carrier B-MACs of the BEBs
Isolated at the edge, invisible to the core
Medium scale, fine-grained policy per MAC
Very large scale, MAC explosion, service provider edges
The cost is real: one more encapsulation layer, so the usable MTU shrinks again; more moving parts, so troubleshooting now has two MAC layers to inspect.
Deploy it when the MAC table is the measured bottleneck — not because it looks more scalable on a slide. Choosing it otherwise is the over-design trap from Chapter 1.
Test: can you name the number of customer MACs per EVI today? If not, you are not yet at the point where PBB-EVPN pays for itself.
